questions.question: Quant Speed Blitz: Compute 35² (35 × 35) mentally.
questions.explanation: To square any number ending in 5: multiply the first digit n by (n+1), then append 25. 3 × 4 = 12 -> 1225.
questions.hintText: Multiply 3 × (3 + 1) = 12, then attach 25 at the end!

questions.question: Two fair 6-sided dice are rolled. How many of the 36 outcomes sum to exactly 7?
questions.explanation: The pairs summing to 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) — exactly 6 outcomes.
questions.hintText: For any first die roll (1..6), there is exactly 1 matching value on the second die.

questions.question: Rule of 72: At an 8% annual compound return, approximately how many years does it take to double your portfolio?
questions.explanation: By the Rule of 72: Years to double ≈ 72 / Interest Rate = 72 / 8 = 9 years.
questions.hintText: Divide 72 by the annual percentage rate (8).

questions.question: Mental Combinatorics: How many handshakes occur if 10 people in a room each shake hands with everyone else once?
questions.explanation: n(n - 1) / 2 = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 unique handshakes.
questions.hintText: Compute 10 choose 2 = (10 × 9) / 2.

questions.question: Mental Math Trick: What is 45² (45 × 45) calculated instantly?
questions.explanation: Rule for numbers ending in 5: 4 × (4 + 1) = 20, attach 25 -> 2025.
questions.hintText: Multiply 4 by 5 (= 20) and append 25.

questions.question: Speed Multiplication: What is 34 × 11 computed in your head?
questions.explanation: Insert sum of digits (3 + 4 = 7) between 3 and 4 -> 374.
questions.hintText: Put 3 + 4 = 7 between 3 and 4.

questions.question: Rule of 72: At an interest rate of 6% compounded annually, about how many years will it take for an investment to double?
questions.explanation: Rule of 72: Years = 72 / rate = 72 / 6 = 12 years.
questions.hintText: Divide 72 by 6.

questions.question: Speed Squaring: What is 65² (65 × 65)?
questions.hintText: Multiply 6 × 7 and append 25.

questions.question: Probability: What is the probability of flipping two heads in two independent fair coin flips?
questions.hintText: Multiply 1/2 by 1/2.

questions.question: Mental Division by 25: What is 1200 / 25 calculated quickly?
questions.explanation: Dividing by 25 is multiplying by 4 and dividing by 100: (1200 × 4) / 100 = 4800 / 100 = 48.
questions.hintText: Multiply 12 by 4.

questions.question: Speed Squaring: What is 85² (85 × 85)?
questions.hintText: Multiply 8 × 9 and append 25.

questions.question: Expected Value: A game pays $10 with probability 0.5 and $0 with probability 0.5. What is the expected value E[X]?
questions.hintText: Half of 10.

questions.question: Close to 100 Multiplication: What is 103 × 105 computed mentally?
Geometric Distribution: Flipping a fair coin until you see Heads. What is the EXPECTED number of flips required?
questions.explanation: For a geometric distribution with p = 0.5, expected trials E[N] = 1/p = 1/0.5 = 2 flips.
questions.hintText: Formula: 1 / p where p is probability of success (1 / 0.5).

questions.question: Close to 100 Under: What is 98 × 96 computed mentally?
questions.hintText: Subtract 4 from 98 (= 94) and append (-2) × (-4) = 08.

questions.question: Options Trading: What is the DELTA of a Call option that is deep in-the-money (almost certain to be exercised)?
questions.explanation: Deep in-the-money call options move dollar-for-dollar with the underlying asset, having a delta approaching +1.0.
questions.hintText: Moves 1:1 with the stock price.

questions.question: Speed Squaring: What is 95² (95 × 95)?
Kelly Criterion: If a bet has 60% win rate (p = 0.6) paying 1:1 (b = 1), what fraction f* of your bankroll should you bet according to Kelly (f = (bp - q) / b)?
Quant Finance: Which Greek measures the rate of decay of an option's price over time (time decay)?
questions.explanation: Theta represents the sensitivity of the option's value to the passage of time (daily decay).
questions.hintText: Starts with T like Time.

questions.question: Bayesian Update: Disease affects 1% of population. Test has 90% true positive and 10% false positive. If a random person tests positive, what is the approximate probability they actually have the disease?
questions.hintText: Base rate fallacy: false positives from the 99% healthy dominate the true positives from the 1%.

questions.question: Finance Ratios: The Sharpe Ratio of an investment portfolio is calculated as:
questions.optionsString: (Return - Benchmark) / Beta|(Portfolio Return - Risk-Free Rate) / Portfolio Volatility (σ)|Total Profit / Total Loss|Dividend Yield / Price
questions.explanation: Sharpe Ratio = (R_p - R_f) / σ_p, measuring risk-adjusted excess return per unit of volatility.
questions.hintText: Excess return divided by standard deviation (volatility).

questions.question: Mental Math Product: What is 125 × 32 computed mentally without a calculator?
questions.hintText: 125 is 1000 / 8, so divide 32 by 8 and multiply by 1000.

questions.question: Financial Mathematics: In the Black-Scholes formula, stock price returns are assumed to follow which distribution?
questions.optionsString: Lognormal distribution (geometric Brownian motion)|Uniform distribution|Student's t-distribution with 1 degree of freedom|Binomial distribution
questions.explanation: Black-Scholes assumes underlying asset prices are lognormally distributed with constant volatility.
questions.hintText: Stock prices cannot go below zero, hence lognormal.

questions.question: Birthday Paradox: What is the minimum number of people in a room required for the probability of at least two sharing a birthday to exceed 50%?
questions.explanation: With 23 people, there are C(23, 2) = 253 pairs; the probability of at least one shared birthday exceeds 50.7%.
questions.hintText: Far fewer than half of 365: only twenty-three people.

questions.question: Quantitative Volatility: If an asset has an annual volatility of 16%, what is its daily volatility assuming 256 trading days in a year (Square Root of Time rule)?
questions.explanation: Daily σ = Annual σ / √256 = 16% / 16 = 1.0%.
questions.hintText: Divide by the square root of 256 (which is 16).

questions.question: Combinatorics: What is the number of distinct ways to choose 2 stocks from a universe of 20 stocks (C(20, 2))?
Arbitrage: What is the financial law stating that two assets with identical future cash flows must sell for the same price?
questions.optionsString: The Law of One Price|Fisher's Hypothesis|The Efficient Frontier|Pareto Optimality
questions.explanation: The Law of One Price states identical cash flows must have identical prices; otherwise, risk-free arbitrage exists.
questions.hintText: Law of One Price.

questions.question: Poisson Distribution: If customer orders arrive at an average rate of λ = 3 per minute, what is the variance of the number of arrivals in one minute?
questions.explanation: In a Poisson distribution, the variance Var(X) is equal to the mean λ: Var(X) = λ = 3.
questions.hintText: For a Poisson distribution, variance equals the mean.

questions.question: High-Frequency Trading: What is 'slippage' in algorithmic execution?
questions.optionsString: When a computer network wire physically slides|The fee paid to the broker|The difference between the expected execution price of an order and the actual price at which it fills|A hardware clock drift
questions.explanation: Slippage occurs during market volatility or latency when an order fills at a worse price than anticipated.
questions.hintText: Difference between intended price and actual fill price.

questions.question: Mental Percentage: If a stock falls by 50%, what percentage gain is required from the low to return to the original price?
questions.explanation: If a $100 stock drops to $50, it must gain $50 to reach $100 again. $50 / $50 = 100% gain required.
questions.hintText: From 50 back up to 100 requires doubling (+100%).

questions.question: Risk Management: What does Value at Risk (VaR) at 95% confidence for 1 day equal to $1,000,000 mean?
questions.optionsString: There is a 5% chance that the portfolio will lose more than $1,000,000 over the next day|The portfolio is guaranteed to make $1,000,000 in 95 days|The maximum loss possible is exactly $1,000,000|The portfolio has a 95% chance of zero loss
questions.explanation: 95% 1-day VaR means that in 95 out of 100 days losses will not exceed $1M (5% tail risk).
questions.hintText: 5% probability of exceeding this loss threshold.

questions.question: Martingale St. Petersburg: In a game where payout doubles every flip (2, 4, 8, 16...), what is the theoretical mathematical expectation?
questions.explanation: Sum (1/2)^k × 2^k = 1 + 1 + 1 + ... = Infinity (St. Petersburg paradox).
questions.hintText: 1 + 1 + 1 + ... diverges to infinity.

questions.question: Put-Call Parity: For European options on non-dividend stock, what fundamental relationship links Call (C) and Put (P) with Strike K and Stock S?
questions.optionsString: C + P = S + K|C - P = S - K × e^(-rT)|C × P = S × K|C + S = P - K
questions.explanation: Put-Call Parity: C - P = S - K × e^(-rT) (or C + K×e^(-rT) = P + S).
questions.hintText: Call minus Put equals Stock minus discounted Strike.

questions.question: Approximately how many minutes does it take sunlight to travel 1 AU from the Sun to Earth?
questions.explanation: At c ≈ 300,000 km/s across 150 million km, light takes ~500 seconds ≈ 8.3 minutes.
questions.hintText: 150,000,000 km divided by 300,000 km/s is 500 seconds (~8 minutes).

questions.question: If the distance between two masses is tripled (3r), by what factor does their gravitational attraction decrease (1/N)? Enter N:
questions.explanation: Newton's Universal Gravitation follows an inverse-square law (1/r²). Tripling r reduces force by 3² = 9.
questions.hintText: Gravity obeys the inverse-square law: 3² = ?

questions.question: Earth's escape velocity is approximately how many km/s (rounded to the nearest integer)?
questions.explanation: v_escape = sqrt(2GM/R) ≈ 11.2 km/s (rounded to 11 km/s).
questions.hintText: Low Earth orbit is ~8 km/s; multiply by √2 ≈ 1.414 to get ~11 km/s.

questions.question: Cosmic Expansion: What optical shift in light spectra proved to Edwin Hubble that distant galaxies are moving away from us?
questions.explanation: Due to the Doppler effect on expanding space, emitted light is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths (Redshift).
questions.hintText: Longer wavelengths correspond to the red end of the visible spectrum.

questions.question: Quantum Energy: According to Planck's relation E = h·f, the energy of a photon is directly proportional to its:
questions.explanation: Planck's equation states that photon energy E equals Planck's constant h multiplied by its frequency f.
questions.hintText: Higher frequency (like gamma rays) means much higher photon energy.

questions.question: Stellar Limits: What is the Chandrasekhar limit (~1.4 solar masses)?
questions.optionsString: The minimum mass required for a planet to have rings|The maximum stable mass of a white dwarf before collapsing into a neutron star or supernova|The mass of our Moon|The mass of the supermassive black hole at the galactic center
questions.explanation: Above ~1.4 solar masses, electron degeneracy pressure cannot prevent gravitational collapse in a white dwarf.
questions.hintText: Limit named after Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar for white dwarf collapse.

questions.question: Relativistic Time Dilation: In General Relativity, how does time pass near a massive body (like a neutron star or black hole) compared to deep empty space?
questions.optionsString: Time passes SLOWER near the massive object (gravitational time dilation)|Time passes FASTER near the massive object|Time flows in reverse|Time is completely unaffected by gravity
questions.explanation: Stronger gravitational potential slows down proper time relative to a distant observer (gravitational time dilation).
questions.hintText: Clocks run slower at the bottom of a gravity well.

questions.question: Cosmic Echo: What is the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation with temperature ~2.725 Kelvin?
questions.optionsString: Microwaves emitted by microwave ovens|The thermal remnant radiation left over from the Big Bang (~380,000 years after creation)|Light from nearby stars reflecting off asteroid dust|Signals from alien satellites
questions.explanation: The CMB is ancient relic radiation from the recombination era when the universe first became transparent to light.
questions.hintText: The thermal afterglow of the Big Bang filling the entire cosmos.

questions.question: Schwarzschild Radius: What is the Schwarzschild radius of a non-rotating mass M (formula for the event horizon radius)?
questions.optionsString: r_s = GM / c²|r_s = 2GM / c²|r_s = GM / 2c²|r_s = √(2GM / c)
questions.explanation: The Schwarzschild radius is r_s = 2GM / c², setting escape velocity equal to the speed of light c.
questions.hintText: Derived from ½mv² = GMm/r when v = c.

questions.question: Photoelectric Effect: For which breakthrough discovery did Albert Einstein win the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921?
questions.optionsString: Special Relativity (E = mc²)|General Relativity (Curved spacetime)|Explanation of the Photoelectric Effect using light quanta (photons)|Bose-Einstein Condensation
questions.explanation: Einstein was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize for his law of the photoelectric effect, establishing the quantum nature of light.
questions.hintText: Light behaving as discrete packets of energy (photons).

questions.question: Quantum Tunneling: How do atomic nuclei fuse inside the Sun despite their mutual electrostatic Coulomb repulsion?
questions.optionsString: Quantum tunneling allows protons to penetrate the potential Coulomb barrier|The Sun has a gigantic mechanical compressor|Protons lose their electric charge at 10 million Kelvin|Magnetic field eliminates all electric repulsion
questions.explanation: The core of the Sun (~15M K) is not hot enough for classical fusion; quantum tunneling allows protons to overcome the Coulomb barrier.
questions.hintText: Wave-particle duality allows particles to 'tunnel' through energetic walls.

questions.question: Quantum Entanglement: What did Albert Einstein famously call quantum entanglement due to its non-local correlation across space?
questions.optionsString: Cosmic harmony|Spooky action at a distance (spukhafte Fernwirkung)|The holographic mirror|Wavefunction hallucination
questions.explanation: Einstein was uncomfortable with instantaneous non-local state collapse and called it 'spooky action at a distance'.
questions.hintText: 'Spooky action at a distance'.

questions.question: De Broglie Wavelength: What relates the wavelength λ of any matter particle to its linear momentum p (p = m·v)?
questions.optionsString: λ = p / h|λ = h·p|λ = h / p|λ = p² / 2m
questions.explanation: De Broglie's matter wave equation states λ = h / p, where h is Planck's constant and p is momentum.
questions.hintText: Wavelength equals Planck's constant divided by momentum.

questions.question: Black Hole Thermodynamics: What is the theoretical radiation that black holes are predicted to emit due to quantum vacuum fluctuations near the event horizon?
questions.explanation: Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that quantum particle-antiparticle pairs near the horizon cause black holes to slowly radiate and evaporate.
questions.hintText: Named after physicist Stephen Hawking.

questions.question: Bell's Theorem: What do experimental violations of Bell's inequalities definitively prove about our universe?
questions.optionsString: The universe cannot be both local AND realistic (local hidden variables are ruled out)|The speed of light can be exceeded by spaceships|Electrons do not possess spin|Gravity does not exist at micro-scales
questions.explanation: John Bell proved that quantum predictions conflict with local hidden variable theories; tests prove the universe is fundamentally non-local.
questions.hintText: Local realism is refuted by quantum mechanics.

questions.question: Relativistic Momentum: As a particle with mass approaches the speed of light (v -> c), what happens to its relativistic momentum and energy?
questions.optionsString: They remain constant|They drop to zero|They asymptotically approach INFINITY (requiring infinite energy to reach c)|They turn negative
questions.explanation: The Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 - v²/c²) diverges to infinity as v approaches c, preventing any mass from reaching c.
questions.hintText: The Lorentz factor gamma tends to infinity.

questions.question: Neutron Stars: What outward quantum pressure halts the gravitational collapse in a neutron star?
questions.optionsString: Thermal gas pressure|Neutron degeneracy pressure (Pauli exclusion principle for neutrons)|Electron repulsion|Electromagnetic radiation pressure
questions.explanation: Neutron degeneracy pressure, governed by the Pauli Exclusion Principle for fermions, supports the neutron star against gravity.
questions.hintText: Pauli exclusion principle applied to closely packed neutrons.

questions.question: General Relativity: How does Einstein's theory of gravity describe the gravitational orbit of Earth around the Sun?
questions.optionsString: Earth moves along a straight geodesic in curved 4-dimensional spacetime warped by the Sun's mass|An invisible magnetic tether pulls Earth|Subatomic gravitons physically push Earth like wind|Earth is suspended in liquid ether
questions.explanation: Mass tells spacetime how to curve; spacetime tells mass how to move along geodesics.
questions.hintText: Geodesics in 4D curved spacetime.

questions.question: Dark Energy: What percentage of the total mass-energy budget of the observable universe is estimated to consist of Dark Energy?
questions.explanation: Dark Energy constitutes ~68%, Dark Matter ~27%, and ordinary baryonic matter is only about 5%.
questions.hintText: About two thirds of the total universe (~68%).

questions.question: Quantum Spin: What is the spin quantum number of all fermions (such as electrons, quarks, protons, and neutrons)?
questions.explanation: Fermions obey Fermi-Dirac statistics and possess half-integer spin (electrons have spin 1/2). Bosons have integer spin.
questions.hintText: Half-integer spin.

questions.question: Stellar Nucleosynthesis: What is the heaviest chemical element that can be produced in the core of a massive star via exothermic nuclear fusion before it collapses into a supernova?
questions.explanation: Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon; fusing iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it, triggering gravitational collapse.
questions.hintText: Iron (symbol Fe, element 26).

questions.question: Speed of Light Limit: Why can NO object with mass reach or exceed the speed of light in vacuum?
questions.optionsString: Its relativistic mass-energy would become infinite, requiring infinite energy to accelerate|Friction with dark matter halts it|Light photons block its path physically|Its size expands beyond the universe
questions.explanation: As v approaches c, gamma factor γ = 1/√(1 - v²/c²) approaches infinity, demanding infinite work.
questions.hintText: Infinite energy would be required to reach c.

questions.question: Gravitational Lensing: What happens when light from a distant quasar passes close to a massive galaxy cluster?
questions.optionsString: The light slows down to a complete halt|The light's path is bent by spacetime curvature, creating magnified, distorted, or multiple Einstein ring images|The light is converted into radio waves|The light turns into dark matter
questions.explanation: Gravitational lensing acts as a cosmic magnifying glass, bending photon trajectories around massive spacetime distortions.
questions.hintText: Spacetime curvature acts as a gravitational lens.

questions.question: Thermodynamics in Cosmology: What does the Second Law of Thermodynamics imply about the ultimate fate of the universe in the 'Heat Death' scenario?
questions.optionsString: Entropy will decrease to zero|Entropy will reach a maximum where all thermal gradients are exhausted and no usable work can be extracted|All stars will re-ignite simultaneously|The temperature will reach infinity
questions.explanation: At maximum cosmic entropy, all energy is evenly distributed at uniform temperature, ending all thermodynamic work.
questions.hintText: Maximum entropy means no thermodynamic gradients left.

questions.question: Quantum Superposition: In the Schrödinger's Cat thought experiment, what causes the cat's state to resolve from a superposition to a definite outcome in the Copenhagen interpretation?
questions.optionsString: Decoherence by heat|The passage of 1 hour|The act of measurement/observation (wavefunction collapse)|Nuclear decay
questions.explanation: In the Copenhagen interpretation, physical measurement collapses the wave function |ψ⟩ into an eigenstate.
questions.hintText: Wavefunction collapse upon observation.

questions.question: Hubble's Constant: What does Hubble's Constant H₀ measure?
questions.optionsString: The expansion rate of the universe (velocity per unit distance, ~70 km/s/Mpc)|The total mass of the Milky Way|The temperature of the sun's corona|The speed of gravitational waves
questions.explanation: Hubble's constant relates recession velocity to distance: v = H₀ × d, measuring cosmic expansion.
questions.hintText: Recession speed divided by megaparsecs of distance.

questions.question: Higgs Boson: What fundamental property does the Higgs field impart to elementary particles (like quarks and W/Z bosons) through their interaction with it?
questions.optionsString: Electric charge|Rest mass|Color charge|Magnetic dipole moment
questions.explanation: Particles gain inertial mass through the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism by interacting with the non-zero vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field.
questions.hintText: It is often called the mass-giving mechanism.

questions.question: General Relativity Tests: What minute anomaly in Mercury's orbit could NOT be explained by Newtonian gravity, but was precisely predicted by Einstein's General Relativity?
questions.optionsString: Its orbital period was slowing down|The anomalous perihelion precession of 43 arcseconds per century|Its moons were disappearing|Its magnetic field was flipping
questions.explanation: The curvature of spacetime near the Sun accounts for the extra 43 arcseconds per century in Mercury's perihelion shift.
questions.hintText: Precession of the perihelion by 43 arcseconds per century.

questions.question: Gravitational Waves: Gravitational waves, directly detected by LIGO in 2015 from colliding black holes, propagate through space at what speed?
questions.optionsString: The speed of light in vacuum (c)|Infinite speed|Speed of sound|Half the speed of light
questions.explanation: In General Relativity, ripples in the curvature of spacetime propagate at exactly the speed of light c.
questions.hintText: Exactly speed of light c.

questions.question: Quantum Electrodynamics: What virtual force-carrier particle mediates the electromagnetic force between charged particles in QED?
questions.explanation: In quantum electrodynamics (QED), electromagnetic interactions occur through the exchange of virtual photons.
questions.hintText: Light particles mediate electromagnetism.

questions.question: Planck Scale: What is the fundamental physical significance of the Planck Length (~1.616 × 10⁻³⁵ meters)?
questions.optionsString: The size of a hydrogen atom|The diameter of a quark|The scale at which quantum gravitational effects dominate and classical spacetime concepts break down|The wavelength of visible light
questions.explanation: Below the Planck scale, quantum fluctuations of spacetime geometry become so severe that smooth manifolds cease to exist.
questions.hintText: The quantum limit where space and time itself become foam-like.

questions.question: Bose-Einstein Condensate: What bizarre macroscopic quantum state occurs when bosons are cooled to temperatures within nanokelvins of absolute zero?
questions.optionsString: They vaporize explosively|A large fraction of atoms collapse into the lowest quantum ground state, behaving as a single macroscopic quantum wave|They turn into antimatter|Their mass becomes infinite
questions.explanation: In a BEC, millions of bosons lose individual identity and merge into a coherent macroscopic quantum super-atom.
questions.hintText: Atoms merge into a single super-wave at lowest ground state.

questions.question: Pauli Exclusion Principle: What fundamental quantum rule dictates that no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously?
questions.optionsString: Heisenberg's matrix|The Pauli Exclusion Principle|Fermi's golden rule|Newton's 3rd law
questions.explanation: Wolfgang Pauli showed that multi-fermion wavefunctions must be anti-symmetric under particle exchange, giving matter stability and volume.
questions.hintText: Formulated by Wolfgang Pauli.

packs.subtitle: Graph theory, concurrency, memory complexity & Kotlin/Python internals
packs.author: Systems Architecture Guild

questions.question: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height H=3 (where a single root node has height 1)?
questions.explanation: A full binary tree of height H has 2^H - 1 nodes. For H=3: 2³ - 1 = 7 nodes.
questions.hintText: Sum of powers of 2: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

questions.question: Which data structure guarantees O(1) average-time lookup AND preserves insertion order in Kotlin/Java?
questions.explanation: LinkedHashMap maintains a doubly-linked list running through its hash buckets, giving O(1) lookup with predictable insertion order.
questions.hintText: It combines a Hash table with a Linked list.

questions.question: In distributed systems, the CAP Theorem states a system during a network partition (P) must trade off between:
questions.explanation: Brewer's CAP Theorem states that in the presence of a Network Partition (P), a distributed data store must choose between Consistency (C) and Availability (A).
questions.hintText: What do the 'C' and 'A' in CAP stand for?

questions.question: Sorting Algorithms: What is the optimal time complexity of comparison-based sorting (like MergeSort) in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Mathematically proven via decision trees: comparison-based sorts require Ω(n log n) operations in the worst case.
questions.hintText: n log n is the lower bound for comparison sorting.

questions.question: Graph Traversal: Which graph search algorithm uses a Queue and explores level-by-level to guarantee the shortest path in unweighted graphs?
questions.optionsString: Breadth-First Search (BFS)|Depth-First Search (DFS)|Dijkstra's with negative weights|Topological Sort
questions.explanation: BFS traverses nodes layer by layer using a FIFO queue, finding shortest paths on unweighted graphs.
questions.hintText: Breadth-first search explores neighboring nodes first.

questions.question: Tree Traversal: An In-Order traversal (Left -> Node -> Right) on a valid Binary Search Tree produces values in what order?
questions.explanation: In a BST, Left < Node < Right; traversing In-Order inherently yields elements in sorted ascending order.
questions.hintText: Left is smaller, Right is greater, so Left-Node-Right is ascending.

questions.question: Data Structures: What is the average-case lookup time in a well-distributed Hash Table?
questions.explanation: A hash function computes bucket index directly, offering O(1) constant average lookup time.
questions.hintText: Instant lookup in constant time.

questions.question: Recursion: What essential component must every recursive function have to prevent infinite recursion and a StackOverflowError?
questions.optionsString: Base case (termination condition)|A global variable|A while loop|A thread lock
questions.explanation: A base case returns a value without making further recursive calls, unwinding the call stack.
questions.hintText: Condition where recursion stops.

questions.question: LRU Cache: What combination of two data structures implements an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache with O(1) get and put?
questions.optionsString: Binary Tree + Array|Hash Map + Doubly Linked List|Stack + Queue|Red-Black Tree + Heap
questions.explanation: HashMap gives O(1) key-to-node lookup, while a Doubly Linked List allows O(1) node removal and insertion to the front.
questions.hintText: Hash Map provides instant lookup, Doubly Linked List provides instant reordering.

questions.question: Graph Algorithms: Which greedy algorithm finds the single-source shortest paths in a directed graph with NON-NEGATIVE edge weights?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm uses a priority queue to iteratively expand the closest unvisited node on graphs with non-negative weights.
questions.hintText: Formulated by Edsger W. Dijkstra.

questions.question: Dynamic Programming: What two core properties indicate that a problem is best solved using Dynamic Programming?
questions.optionsString: Optimal Substructure and Overlapping Subproblems|Randomized Inputs and Infinite Recursion|Sorted arrays and Prime factors|Greedy Choice and Constant Time
questions.explanation: DP applies when an optimal solution can be constructed from optimal solutions to overlapping subproblems.
questions.hintText: Optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems.

questions.question: Prefix Trees (Tries): Why are Tries exceptionally well-suited for autocomplete search engines?
questions.optionsString: They use less memory than integers|Prefix search takes O(L) time proportional only to the word length L, independent of the total dictionary size N|They automatically encrypt data|They avoid all pointer overhead
questions.explanation: In a Trie, traversing to find all words with prefix of length L takes O(L) time regardless of how many million words exist.
questions.hintText: Lookup time depends only on word length, not database size.

questions.question: Two Pointers: In the famous 'Two Sum II' problem on a SORTED array, how do two pointers find the target sum in O(n) time and O(1) space?
questions.optionsString: By sorting the array again|By moving both pointers from left to right|Start one at index 0 and one at n-1: if sum < target, advance left; if sum > target, decrement right|By using nested loops
questions.explanation: Because the array is sorted, incrementing left increases the sum, and decrementing right decreases the sum.
questions.hintText: Pointers at opposite ends closing inward.

questions.question: Sliding Window: What is the optimal time complexity to find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of fixed size K in an array of size N?
questions.explanation: Using sliding window, each step subtracts the element leaving the window and adds the entering element in O(1), making total time O(N).
questions.hintText: Add the incoming element and subtract the outgoing element at each step.

questions.question: Concurrency: What does the Atomic Compare-And-Swap (CAS) instruction enable in lock-free multi-threaded data structures?
questions.optionsString: Atomic updates without locking OS mutexes, retrying if value changed concurrently|Slowing down threads intentionally|Deleting memory automatically|Doubling the CPU cache size
questions.explanation: CAS atomically compares memory location against expected value and updates if matched, enabling lock-free algorithms.
questions.hintText: Lock-free synchronization at the hardware CPU level.

questions.question: Disjoint Set Union (DSU): With both 'Union by Rank' and 'Path Compression' heuristics, what is the nearly constant amortized time complexity per operation?
questions.optionsString: O(log n)|O(α(n)) where α is the inverse Ackermann function|O(n)|O(1) strictly
questions.explanation: Path compression + rank union yields O(α(n)) amortized per operation, where α(n) < 5 for all practical universe sizes.
questions.hintText: Inverse Ackermann function α(n).

questions.question: JVM Internals: What is the fundamental rationale behind the 'Generational Hypothesis' utilized by modern Garbage Collectors (G1, ZGC)?
questions.optionsString: All objects live forever|Most objects die shortly after creation (infant mortality)|Objects never move between heap areas|Strings take 90% of heap
questions.explanation: Empirical studies prove that the vast majority of allocated objects become garbage very quickly, justifying young/old generational separation.
questions.hintText: Most objects are temporary and die young.

questions.question: Distributed Consensus: Which distributed consensus algorithm is widely used in modern cloud orchestrators (like Kubernetes etcd and HashiCorp Raft)?
questions.explanation: Raft is designed for understandability while providing full Paxos-equivalent consensus for leader election and replicated state machines.
questions.hintText: Raft algorithm (leader election + log replication).

questions.question: Trie String Search: What is the time complexity to find the Longest Common Prefix of N strings each of maximum length L using a Trie?
questions.explanation: Inserting N strings takes O(N × L), and traversing down the single-child branch takes O(L) time, giving O(N × L) total.
questions.hintText: Building the trie takes N times L steps.

questions.question: Memory Alignment: Why do modern 64-bit CPU architectures pad struct/class fields to multiples of 4 or 8 bytes?
questions.optionsString: To confuse decompilers|CPUs read memory in cache line word chunks; unaligned memory accesses require multiple memory bus cycles and degrade performance|Memory chips cannot store odd addresses|To prevent buffer overflows automatically
questions.explanation: CPUs access memory efficiently at aligned word boundaries (e.g. 64-bit words); unaligned access penalizes throughput.
questions.hintText: Aligned access allows single-cycle CPU word reading.

questions.question: Topological Sort: On which type of graph is Topological Sort strictly guaranteed to be possible?
questions.optionsString: Any undirected graph|Graphs with negative cycles|Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)|Complete bipartite graphs only
questions.explanation: Topological sort is possible if and only if the directed graph has NO cycles (it is a DAG).
questions.hintText: Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).

questions.question: Bloom Filter: What type of error can a standard Bloom Filter produce?
questions.optionsString: False Negatives only|False Positives only (may claim an item is present when it isn't)|Both False Positives and False Negatives|Zero errors ever
questions.explanation: A Bloom filter guarantees no false negatives: if it says 'not present', it is definitely not. But hash collisions can yield false positives.
questions.hintText: It never produces false negatives, only false positives.

questions.question: Dynamic Programming: What is the optimal time complexity of solving the 0/1 Knapsack Problem with N items and maximum weight capacity W?
questions.explanation: The standard DP table has dimensions (N + 1) × (W + 1), evaluated in pseudo-polynomial O(N × W) time.
questions.hintText: Pseudo-polynomial time O(N × W).

questions.question: Operating Systems: What is 'Thrashing' in virtual memory systems?
questions.optionsString: Hard drive physically vibrating|A state where the CPU spends more time swapping virtual memory pages to disk than executing actual instructions|Network packet loss exceeding 50%|Rapid thread deletion
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when high memory pressure causes continuous page faults, grinding the system to a halt.
questions.hintText: Excessive page swapping to disk choking the CPU.

questions.question: Kotlin Internals: What bytecode transformation does the Kotlin compiler apply to an `inline` function with reified type parameters?
questions.optionsString: Creates a separate subclass per type|Uses reflection at runtime for every call|Pastes the function body directly at call sites, substituting the concrete class token for the reified generic|Converts the function into a C++ pointer
questions.explanation: Inlining copies the bytecode directly into the call site, allowing exact type access despite JVM type erasure.
questions.hintText: Replaces the call site with direct bytecode, bypassing type erasure.

questions.question: Tree Structures: What is the main operational advantage of a B-Tree over a Red-Black Tree in database indexing (e.g. Postgres / SQLite)?
questions.optionsString: High branching factor minimizes disk I/O reads by packing many keys into each page-sized node|B-Trees use zero memory pointers|B-Trees cannot store duplicate keys|Red-Black trees cannot be balanced
questions.explanation: B-Trees have wide nodes matching disk page sizes (4KB-16KB), drastically reducing expensive disk seeks.
questions.hintText: High branching factor matches block storage and minimizes disk reads.

questions.question: Bit Manipulation: What fast operation checks if a positive integer N is an exact power of 2 (e.g. 2, 4, 8, 16)?
questions.explanation: Powers of 2 have only 1 bit set (e.g. 1000₂). N - 1 has all lower bits set (0111₂). (N & (N - 1)) == 0.
questions.hintText: Bitwise AND with (N - 1).

questions.question: Database Isolation: What concurrency anomaly occurs when Transaction A reads a row, Transaction B updates that row and commits, and Transaction A reads it again getting different values?
questions.explanation: A Non-Repeatable Read occurs when re-reading the same committed row produces modified data.
questions.hintText: The same read cannot be repeated consistently.

questions.question: Network Protocols: Why does TCP establish connections using a 3-Way Handshake (SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK)?
questions.optionsString: To synchronize Initial Sequence Numbers (ISNs) and confirm bidirectional communication capability|To encrypt all payload data|To allocate IP addresses dynamically|To prevent physical wire interference
questions.explanation: The 3-way handshake verifies both endpoints can send and receive, agreeing on initial packet sequence numbers.
questions.hintText: Confirms two-way readiness and syncs sequence numbers.

questions.question: Kotlin Coroutines: Which dispatcher should be used in Kotlin for offloading disk I/O or network API requests to prevent blocking the UI thread?
questions.explanation: Dispatchers.IO uses an elastic thread pool specifically designed for blocking I/O calls.
questions.hintText: IO stands for Input/Output.

questions.question: Consistent Hashing: How does Consistent Hashing minimize data movement when a new caching node is added to a distributed cluster of N nodes?
questions.optionsString: It rehashes all N keys|It deletes older keys|Keys and nodes are mapped onto a 360° ring; adding a node only remaps K/N keys from its immediate neighbor|It stores all keys on all nodes
questions.explanation: On a hash ring, adding a node only shifts keys from its immediate adjacent successor, leaving (N-1)/N of the keys untouched.
questions.hintText: Hash ring where only K/N keys are moved to the new node.

questions.question: CPU Architecture: What is 'False Sharing' in high-performance multi-threaded C++/Java applications?
questions.optionsString: Two threads modifying independent variables that reside on the same 64-byte CPU cache line, causing constant cache invalidations|Threads sharing passwords illegally|A corrupted memory bus|Copying data to a wrong thread
questions.explanation: False sharing occurs when independent variables sit on the same cache line, forcing L1/L2 cache coherence invalidations.
questions.hintText: Independent variables sharing the same hardware cache line.

questions.question: Dynamic Programming: What is the time complexity of the Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) problem using binary search with patience sorting?
questions.explanation: Patience sorting maintains an active array of smallest tails and updates it via binary search in O(n log n) time.
questions.hintText: Binary search on tail array gives n log n.

questions.question: In the classic Monty Hall 3-door problem, if you switch doors after the host reveals a goat, what is your probability of winning the car?
questions.explanation: Your initial pick is wrong 2/3 of the time. Whenever your initial pick is wrong, the host is forced to reveal the only other goat, so switching wins 2/3 of the time!
questions.hintText: Your first choice had a 1/3 chance; the remaining 2/3 probability concentrates into the single unopened door.

questions.question: You have 8 identical-looking gold coins, but 1 is slightly heavier. Using a two-pan balance scale, what is the minimum number of weighings needed to guarantee finding the heavy coin?
questions.explanation: Weigh 3 against 3. If balanced, weigh the remaining 2 (1 vs 1). If unbalanced, take the heavier 3 and weigh 1 vs 1. Only 2 weighings needed!
questions.hintText: Each weighing has 3 outcomes (Left, Right, Balanced), so k weighings can distinguish up to 3^k coins (3² = 9 ≥ 8).

questions.question: The River Crossing: A farmer must transport a wolf, a goat, and a cabbage across a river in a boat that can only carry him and ONE item. Which item must he take across FIRST?
questions.optionsString: The wolf|The goat|The cabbage|He can go alone
questions.explanation: The wolf will not eat the cabbage. Leaving the wolf with the goat or the goat with the cabbage is fatal, so the goat must cross first.
questions.hintText: The goat is the common danger (eats cabbage, eaten by wolf).

questions.question: Water Jug Riddle: You have an unmarked 5-liter jug, a 3-liter jug, and an unlimited water tap. How do you measure EXACTLY 4 liters?
questions.optionsString: Fill 3L, pour into 5L twice to overflow|Fill 5L, pour 1L out by eye|Fill 5L, pour into 3L (leaving 2L in 5L). Empty 3L, pour the 2L into 3L. Fill 5L and pour into 3L until full (pouring 1L), leaving 4L in 5L|It is mathematically impossible
questions.explanation: 5 - 3 = 2L. Transfer 2L to 3L jug. Fill 5L. Pour 1L into 3L jug to fill it -> exactly 4L remains in the 5L jug.
questions.hintText: Die Hard 3 water jug puzzle: 5 - 3 leaves 2L, leading to 4L.

questions.question: The Heavy Coin: You have 9 identical-looking gold coins, but 1 is counterfeit and slightly heavier. What is the MINIMUM number of balance scale weighings to guarantee finding it?
questions.explanation: Weigh 3 vs 3. If balanced, coin is in remaining 3. Then weigh 1 vs 1 from that group -> 2 weighings total (3² = 9).
questions.hintText: Split into 3 groups of 3 (3² = 9).

questions.question: Lateral Riddle: A man pushes his car to a hotel and immediately realizes he is bankrupt. Why?
questions.optionsString: His car engine exploded outside the Ritz|He is playing Monopoly and landed on an opponent's hotel property|He had all his cash in the trunk which was stolen|The hotel valet fees were too high
questions.explanation: Classic lateral thinking puzzle: the man is playing the board game Monopoly.
questions.hintText: Think of board games with tiny cars and hotels.

questions.question: Pill Logic: A doctor gives a patient 3 pills and instructs them to take one every 30 minutes. How many minutes will the pills last?
questions.explanation: Pill 1 at 0 min, Pill 2 at 30 min, Pill 3 at 60 min -> 60 minutes total.
questions.hintText: Pill 1 is taken immediately at time 0.

questions.question: Two Doors with Guards: One guard always lies, one always tells truth. What single question asked to either guard reveals the safe door?
questions.optionsString: 'Are you the liar?'|'Which door would the OTHER guard say is the safe door?'|'Is this door safe?'|'Do you like gold?'
questions.explanation: The truth-teller truthfully reports the liar's lie (bad door). The liar lies about the truth-teller's answer (bad door). Both point to the bad door, so take the OTHER door!
questions.hintText: Ask what the OTHER guard would answer.

questions.question: Bridge Crossing at Night: 4 people cross a rope bridge at night with 1 flashlight. Cross times: 1, 2, 5, 10 min. Bridge holds at most 2 people. What is the MINIMUM total time to cross?
questions.explanation: 1 & 2 cross (2 min). 1 returns (1 min). 5 & 10 cross together (10 min). 2 returns (2 min). 1 & 2 cross (2 min). 2 + 1 + 10 + 2 + 2 = 17 min.
questions.hintText: Send the two slowest together (5 and 10) so their times overlap.

questions.question: Burning Ropes Timer: You have two ropes that each take exactly 60 minutes to burn completely, but burn at non-uniform speeds. How do you measure EXACTLY 45 minutes?
questions.optionsString: Cut both ropes with scissors at 3/4 length|Burn one rope end to end, then blow it out|Light rope 1 from BOTH ends and rope 2 from ONE end. When rope 1 finishes (30 min), light the other end of rope 2 (burning in 15 more min) -> 45 min total|It cannot be done due to non-uniform burning
questions.explanation: Burning from both ends halves burn time to 30 min. Lighting the remaining end of rope 2 burns its remaining 30 min in 15 min. 30 + 15 = 45 min.
questions.hintText: Burning a rope from both ends burns it twice as fast (30 min).

questions.question: The 2-Egg Drop Problem: From a 100-story building, what is the MINIMUM number of drops in the worst case to determine the highest floor from which an egg can drop without breaking?
questions.explanation: Triangular numbers: n + (n - 1) + ... + 1 ≥ 100. For n = 14: 14 × 15 / 2 = 105 ≥ 100. Dropping at floors 14, 27, 39... gives worst-case 14 drops.
questions.hintText: Find the smallest n where n(n+1)/2 >= 100.

questions.question: Game Theory: In the classic Prisoner's Dilemma, what is the dominant strategy Nash Equilibrium for both rational suspects?
questions.optionsString: Both stay silent (Cooperate)|Both betray each other (Defect)|Flip a coin|Alternate each round
questions.explanation: Regardless of what the partner chooses, defecting yields a better individual payoff, making (Defect, Defect) the Nash equilibrium.
questions.hintText: Individual self-interest leads both to confess/defect.

questions.question: 100 Prisoners and Boxes: 100 prisoners numbered 1-100 must each find their number in 1 of 50 chosen boxes. What strategy gives them >30% survival probability?
questions.optionsString: Each picks 50 boxes at random|All prisoners open the exact same 50 boxes|Loop strategy: each prisoner starts with the box of their own number, then opens the box indicated by the number inside (following cycles)|Mathematical impossibility (probability is 0.5^100 ≈ 0)
questions.explanation: Following permutation cycles ensures everyone succeeds if the longest cycle is ≤ 50, which occurs with probability 1 - ln(2) ≈ 31.18%.
questions.hintText: Follow the permutation loops starting with your own number.

questions.question: Pirate Game Theory: 5 rational, greedy pirates (ranked 1 to 5) must distribute 100 gold coins. What is the optimal allocation proposed by the senior pirate (Pirate 1)?
questions.optionsString: 98 coins to himself, 0 to Pirate 2, 1 to Pirate 3, 0 to Pirate 4, 1 to Pirate 5|20 coins to each pirate equally|50 coins to himself, 50 to Pirate 5|96 coins to himself, 1 to everyone else
questions.explanation: By backward induction, pirates 3 and 5 will receive 0 in the 4-pirate and 2-pirate subgames, so 1 coin secures their vote (giving Pirate 1 three votes needed for majority).
questions.hintText: Backward induction: buy off pirates who would otherwise get zero.

questions.question: The Blue Eyes Island: On an island with 100 blue-eyed people, a visitor announces publicly: 'At least one of you has blue eyes.' What happens on the 100th day?
questions.optionsString: Nothing happens|All 100 blue-eyed people deduce their eye color and leave the island simultaneously|Only the oldest person leaves|One person leaves every day
questions.explanation: Common knowledge induction: by day K, if no one left, there must be at least K+1 blue-eyed people. On day 100, all 100 deduce their own eyes are blue and depart.
questions.hintText: Induction up to day 100: common knowledge forces simultaneous realization.

questions.question: Missing Dollar Riddle: 3 men pay $30 for a room ($10 each). Manager refunds $5. Bellboy pockets $2 and returns $1 to each man (they paid $9 each = $27). $27 + $2 = $29. Where is the missing $1?
questions.optionsString: The addition is flawed: the $2 was KEPT from the $27, not added to it ($27 paid = $25 hotel + $2 bellboy)|The hotel manager has it|The bellboy stole $3|It evaporated in taxes
questions.explanation: Total paid is $27: $25 to hotel + $2 to bellboy. Adding the bellboy's $2 to $27 is a meaningless double-count fallacy.
questions.hintText: Subtract the bellboy's $2 from the $27 to get the $25 room cost.

questions.question: The 12 Coins Weighing Problem: With 12 coins where 1 is counterfeit (either heavier OR lighter), what is the MINIMUM number of balance scale weighings to identify the coin and its weight?
questions.explanation: 3 weighings give 3³ = 27 outcomes, which is sufficient to identify 1 of 12 coins and whether it is heavier or lighter (24 outcomes).
questions.hintText: 3 weighings yield 27 ternary outcomes; 2 × 12 = 24 possibilities.

questions.question: Chessboard Domination: What is the maximum number of Queens that can be placed on an 8×8 chessboard such that no two Queens attack each other (The 8-Queens Puzzle)?
questions.explanation: Because each Queen requires its own row and column, at most 8 Queens can be placed without attacking each other.
questions.hintText: One Queen per row on an 8-row board.

questions.question: Airplane Fuel Around the World: Planes have tanks holding fuel for half a world trip. They can transfer fuel in flight. What is the MINIMUM number of planes required for one plane to circle the globe and all return safely?
questions.explanation: 3 planes take off together. Plane A transfers fuel to B & C and returns. Plane B transfers to C and returns. Plane C circles and meets returning support.
questions.hintText: 3 planes sharing fuel at 1/8 and 1/4 mark.

questions.question: Fox, Goose, Bag of Grain: Why is this river puzzle structurally identical to the Wolf, Goat, and Cabbage puzzle?
questions.optionsString: Because grain eats geese|Fox eats Goose, Goose eats Grain — identical predator-prey-resource graph isomorphism|Because boats are wooden|It is completely different
questions.explanation: The conflict graph A-B-C is mathematically isomorphic: A attacks B, B eats C, while A and C are mutually peaceful.
questions.hintText: The constraint graph has the exact same structure.

questions.question: Horse Race Tournament: You have 25 horses and a 5-lane track (no stopwatch, only relative finish order). What is the MINIMUM races needed to find the TOP 3 fastest horses?
questions.explanation: 5 group races + 1 winner's race (6th). Take top 3 of winner's race and their related candidates -> 1 final race (7th race). Exactly 7 races.
questions.hintText: 5 initial races + 1 race of winners + 1 tie-breaker race = 7.

questions.question: The Poisoned Wine: 1,000 wine bottles, exactly 1 is poisoned. Test strips show poison within 24 hours. How many test strips are needed to find the bottle in 24 hours?
questions.explanation: Each bottle's number is written in 10-bit binary. Each strip drinks from all bottles where its corresponding bit is 1. The binary pattern of positive strips identifies the bottle.
questions.hintText: Binary encoding: 2¹⁰ = 1024 > 1000.

questions.question: Lateral Matchstick: A Roman numeral math equation made of matchsticks reads: XI + I = X (11 + 1 = 10). Without removing or adding matchsticks, how do you make it correct?
questions.optionsString: Turn the equation upside down (it reads X = I + IX: 10 = 1 + 9)|Break a match in half|Move one match to make XII|Set it on fire
questions.explanation: Viewing the equation from the opposite side rotates it 180° into X = I + IX (10 = 1 + 9).
questions.hintText: Rotate your perspective by 180 degrees.

questions.question: Riddle of the Sphinx: What creature walks on 4 legs in the morning, 2 legs at noon, and 3 legs in the evening?
questions.optionsString: A dog|A human (crawling baby, walking adult, elderly with cane)|A Sphinx|A horse
questions.explanation: A human: baby crawls on 4, adult walks on 2, elderly walks with a walking cane on 3.
questions.hintText: The stages of a human life.

questions.question: Monty Hall 4 Doors: There are 4 doors (1 car, 3 goats). You pick Door 1. Host opens Door 2 revealing a goat and offers a switch. What is the probability of winning if you switch?
questions.explanation: Initial pick has 1/4 chance. The remaining 3/4 probability is now split equally between the 2 remaining closed doors: (3/4) / 2 = 3/8 (37.5%).
questions.hintText: 3/4 probability divided among the remaining 2 unpicked doors.

questions.question: The Blind Barman Problem: 4 glasses on a spinning turntable can be face-up or face-down. In each turn, the blindfolded barman can flip any number of glasses, then the table is spun. What guarantees all 4 glasses face the same way?
questions.optionsString: An 7-step algorithmic sequence exploring symmetric configurations|Random flipping|Spinning the table faster|Impossible without vision
questions.explanation: A deterministic state machine algorithm guarantees reaching the all-same state within 7 steps.
questions.hintText: A deterministic algorithm using diagonal and adjacent flips.

questions.question: Riddle of the Heavy Brick: A brick weighs 1 kg plus half a brick. How many kilograms does one brick weigh?
questions.explanation: Equation: B = 1 + 0.5B => 0.5B = 1 => B = 2 kg.
questions.hintText: If half the brick weighs 1 kg, the whole brick weighs 2 kg.

questions.question: Knights, Knaves, and Spies: Knights tell truth, Knaves lie, Spies can do either. Person A says 'I am a knight', B says 'A is telling the truth', C says 'I am the spy'. Who is C?
questions.explanation: A Knight cannot claim to be the spy (that would be a lie). A Knave cannot claim to be the spy (that would be true if he was, or he claims to be a spy which would be true for the spy). Only the Spy can say 'I am the spy'.
questions.hintText: Can a Knight lie about being a spy? Can a Knave tell truth about being a spy?

questions.question: Einstein's Zebra Puzzle: In the famous logic puzzle with 5 colored houses, nationalities, pets, drinks, and cigarettes, what mathematical deduction method is essential?
questions.optionsString: Constraint Satisfaction with cross-table elimination grid|Random guessing|Binomial theorem|Linear regression
questions.explanation: The zebra puzzle is solved using constraint satisfaction and grid-based logical deduction.
questions.hintText: Constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) using logic grids.

questions.question: The Escalator Riddle: Walking up a moving escalator takes 30 steps. Walking down the same moving escalator (against direction) takes 90 steps. How many steps would you see if it were stopped?
questions.explanation: Let E be speed of escalator and v your speed. Distance = 30(1 + E/v) = 90(1 - E/v). Solving gives E/v = 1/2. Distance = 30 × 1.5 = 45 steps.
questions.hintText: Total steps = 30 × (1 + E) = 90 × (1 - E).

questions.question: Chameleons on an Island: 13 red, 15 green, 17 blue chameleons. When two different colors meet, both change into the third color. Can all chameleons ever become ONE color?
questions.optionsString: Yes, they can all become red|No, because the differences modulo 3 of color counts are invariant and never equal|Yes, they can all become blue|Yes, in 45 steps
questions.explanation: When two colors meet, counts change by -1, -1, +2. Modulo 3 differences: (r - g), (g - b), (b - r) mod 3 are strictly invariant. Since initial counts 13, 15, 17 are 1, 0, 2 mod 3, they can never all be equal.
questions.hintText: Modulo 3 invariant prevents all becoming one color.

questions.question: The Birthday Problem in Lateral Logic: Cheryl's Birthday (May, June, July, August dates). Albert knows month, Bernard knows day. Albert says 'I know Bernard doesn't know'. What does that eliminate?
questions.optionsString: May and June (because they contain the unique dates 18 and 19)|July and August|All odd dates|The entire month of July
questions.explanation: If the date were May 19 or June 18, Bernard would know instantly. Albert knowing Bernard doesn't know proves the month cannot be May or June.
questions.hintText: Months with unique day numbers (18, 19) must be eliminated.

questions.question: Lateral Reasoning: A grandfather, father, and son go fishing. Each catches one fish. Yet they return home with exactly 3 fish in the basket, without losing any. How many fishermen were there?
questions.optionsString: 4 fishermen|3 fishermen (Grandfather is also a father; Father is both a father and a son)|2 fishermen|1 fisherman
questions.explanation: There are only 3 people: Grandfather (father to the father), Father (son to grandfather and father to son), and Son.
questions.hintText: One person holds two generational roles: father and son.

packs.title: English B2 Grammar & Vocab (Українською)
packs.subtitle: Умовні речення, модальні дієслова в минулому, інверсія, герундій та фразові дієслова рівня B2 з поясненнями українською
packs.author: QuizLock Language Lab

questions.question: [B2 • 2nd Conditional] Оберіть правильну форму (нереальна умова теперішнього часу): «Якби я був на твоєму місці, я б прийняв цю пропозицію» — If I ___ you, I would accept that offer.
questions.explanation: Second Conditional: If + Past Simple (were для всіх осіб), would + V1. Після 'If' ніколи не ставиться 'would'.
questions.hintText: Формула 2nd Conditional: If + Past Simple (were), would + V1.

questions.question: [B2 • Used to vs Be used to] «Мені знадобився місяць, щоб звикнути рано вставати» — It took me a month to get used to ___ up early.
questions.explanation: У конструкції 'be / get used to' (звикнути до чогось) частка 'to' є прийменником, тому після неї вживається герундій (V-ing): waking.
questions.hintText: get used to + V-ing (герундій)!

questions.question: [B2 • Contrast Linkers] «Незважаючи на сильний дощ, матч продовжився» — ___ the heavy rain, the match went ahead.
questions.explanation: Перед іменником ('the heavy rain') вживається 'Despite' (без 'of'!) або 'In spite of'. Після 'Although' / 'Even though' потрібне повне речення (підмет + присудок).
questions.hintText: Перед групою іменника без 'of' вживається одне слово на D...

questions.question: [B2 • Phrasal Verbs] Яке фразове дієслово означає «миритися з чимось, терпіти» (tolerate)? — I cannot ___ this constant noise anymore!
questions.optionsString: put up with|come up with|look down on|call off
questions.explanation: 'put up with' = терпіти, миритися з чимось; 'come up with' = придумати ідею; 'look down on' = дивитися зверхньо; 'call off' = скасувати.
questions.hintText: Три слівця: put ___ ___ = tolerate.

questions.question: [B2 • Gerund vs Infinitive] «Він кинув палити два роки тому (припинив цю звичку)» — He stopped ___ two years ago.
questions.explanation: 'stop + V-ing' означає повністю припинити дію або звичку. 'stop + to V' означає зупинитися в дорозі, щоб зробити щось інше.
questions.hintText: Припинити дію = stop + V-ing.

questions.question: [B2 • Collocations: Make vs Do] «Науковці проводять важливе дослідження» — Scientists are ___ important research into renewable energy.
questions.explanation: Стійке словосполучення: 'do research' (проводити дослідження). Зі словом 'research' вживається DO, а не MAKE.
questions.hintText: do research / do homework / do damage.

questions.question: [B2 • Past Perfect Continuous] «Ми чекали вже дві години, коли нарешті прибув автобус» — We ___ for two hours when the bus finally arrived.
questions.optionsString: had been waiting|were waiting|have been waiting|waited
questions.explanation: Дія тривала протягом певного часу ('for two hours') ДО іншої події в минулому ('arrived'), тому вживаємо Past Perfect Continuous: had been waiting.
questions.hintText: Тривалість до моменту в минулому: had been + V-ing.

questions.question: [B2 • Causative] «Мені вчора полагодили ноутбук у сервісі» — I had my laptop ___ yesterday.
questions.explanation: Каузативна конструкція 'have something done' (have + Object + V3) показує, що роботу виконав майстер для нас: had my laptop repaired.
questions.hintText: Формула Causative: have + Object + V3 (3-тя форма).

questions.question: [B2 • Future Continuous] «Завтра о цій порі я летітиму до Лондона» — This time tomorrow, I ___ to London.
questions.optionsString: will be flying|will have flown|am flying|fly
questions.explanation: Маркер 'This time tomorrow' вказує на дію, що буде в процесі у конкретний момент майбутнього — Future Continuous (will be + V-ing).
questions.hintText: Процес у точний момент завтра: will be + V-ing.

questions.question: [B2 • Phrasal Verbs] «Вони вирішили скасувати концерт через шторм» — They decided to ___ the concert because of the storm.
questions.explanation: 'call off' = скасувати (cancel); 'put off' = перенести на пізніше (postpone); 'turn down' = відхилити; 'bring up' = порушити тему / виховати.
questions.hintText: Скасувати = call ___.

questions.question: [B2 • Wish (Present)] «Шкода, що я зараз не знаю її номера телефону» — I wish I ___ her phone number right now.
questions.explanation: Бажання змінити теперішню ситуацію ('right now') передається конструкцією 'I wish + Past Simple': I wish I knew.
questions.hintText: Бажання щодо теперішнього часу: I wish + Past Simple (V2).

questions.question: [B2 • 3rd Conditional] «Якби ти попередив мене вчора, я б не припустився тієї помилки» — If you had warned me yesterday, I ___ that mistake.
questions.optionsString: wouldn't have made|wouldn't make|hadn't made|didn't make
questions.explanation: Third Conditional (нереальне минуле): If + Past Perfect (had warned), would(n't) have + V3 (wouldn't have made).
questions.hintText: Головна частина 3rd Conditional: would(n't) have + V3.
questions.acceptedAnswers: wouldn't have made|would not have made

questions.question: [B2 • Past Modals of Deduction] «Він ніяк не міг бачити тебе вчора в Києві — він був у Варшаві!» — He ___ you in Kyiv yesterday — he was in Warsaw!
questions.optionsString: can't have seen|mustn't have seen|shouldn't have seen|may not see
questions.explanation: 100% впевненість у тому, що дія НЕ могла відбутися в минулому, передається через 'can't / couldn't have + V3' (а НЕ mustn't have).
questions.hintText: Неможливість у минулому: can't have + V3.
questions.acceptedAnswers: can't have seen|cannot have seen|couldn't have seen

questions.question: [B2 • Past Criticism] «Тобі варто було перечитати договір перед підписанням (але ти цього не зробив)» — You ___ the contract before signing it.
questions.optionsString: should have read|must have read|would read|could read
questions.explanation: 'should have + V3' виражає докір або пораду щодо минулого, якої не дотрималися.
questions.hintText: Докір щодо минулого: should have + V3.
questions.acceptedAnswers: should have read|ought to have read

questions.question: [B2 • Causative Continuous] «Зараз ми перефарбовуємо кухню (найняли майстрів)» — We ___ our kitchen repainted right now.
questions.explanation: Каузативна форма у Present Continuous ('right now'): are having + Object ('our kitchen') + V3 ('repainted').
questions.hintText: Present Continuous Causative: am/is/are having + Object + V3.

questions.question: [B2 • Remember + V-ing vs to V] «Я чітко пам'ятаю, як замкнув двері перед виходом» — I clearly remember ___ the door before leaving.
questions.explanation: 'remember + V-ing' означає спогад про дію, яка ВЖЕ відбулася в минулому ('пам'ятаю, як замкнув'). 'remember + to V' — не забути зробити щось.
questions.hintText: Спогад про минулу дію: remember + V-ing.

questions.question: [B2 • Wish + Would] «Як би я хотів, щоб ти перестав постійно скаржитися!» — I wish you ___ complaining all the time!
questions.explanation: Коли нас дратує чиясь поведінка і ми хочемо, щоб інша людина її змінила, вживаємо 'I wish + you/he/she + would + V1'.
questions.hintText: Роздратування чиєюсь звичкою: I wish + Subject + would + V1.

questions.question: [B2 • Future Perfect] «До кінця цього року вона пропрацює в компанії вже десять років» — By the end of this year, she ___ at the company for ten years.
questions.optionsString: will have worked|will work|is working|has worked
questions.explanation: Маркер 'By the end of this year' (до певного моменту в майбутньому) вимагає Future Perfect: will have + V3.
questions.hintText: Маркер 'By...' у майбутньому = will have + V3.
questions.acceptedAnswers: will have worked|will have been working

questions.question: [B2 • Past Habit vs State] «Раніше на цьому розі був старий кінотеатр» — There ___ an old cinema on this corner.
questions.optionsString: used to be|was used to being|got used to be|would be
questions.explanation: Для опису стану в минулому (був кінотеатр), якого більше немає, вживається 'used to + V1' ('used to be'). 'Would' для станів не вживається!
questions.hintText: Минулий стан, якого вже немає: used to + V1.

questions.question: [B2 • Contrast Clauses] «Хоча він мав чудову кваліфікацію, роботу йому не запропонували» — ___ he was highly qualified, he wasn't offered the job.
questions.explanation: Перед підметом і присудком ('he was highly qualified') потрібен сполучник 'Even though' або 'Although'.
questions.hintText: Перед повною граматичною основою (he was...): Even though / Although.

questions.question: [B2 • Suggest Pattern] Оберіть граматично правильне продовження: «Вона запропонувала піти іншим маршрутом» — She suggested ___ a different route.
questions.optionsString: taking|to take|us to take|that we tooks
questions.explanation: Після дієслова 'suggest' вживається або герундій (suggest + V-ing: 'suggested taking'), або 'that + Subject + (should) + V1'. Інфінітив 'suggest to do' — груба помилка!
questions.hintText: Після suggest ніколи не йде інфінітив 'to do' — лише герундій (V-ing)!

questions.question: [B2 • Academic Collocations] «Ми повинні взяти до уваги всі фінансові ризики» — We must ___ all financial risks into account.
questions.explanation: Стійкий вираз рівня B2: 'take something into account' (або 'take into consideration') = взяти до уваги / врахувати.
questions.hintText: ___ into account = врахувати.

questions.question: [B2+ • Mixed Conditional] «Якби я прийняв ту роботу торік, я б зараз жив у Берліні» — If I had accepted that job last year, I ___ in Berlin now.
questions.optionsString: would be living|would have lived|will live|lived
questions.explanation: Mixed Conditional (Past Condition → Present Result): умова в минулому (If + Past Perfect), але результат триває ЗАРАЗ ('now'), тому в головній частині вживаємо 'would + V1 / would be + V-ing'.
questions.hintText: Маркер 'now' у головній частині вимагає would + V1 / would be V-ing!

questions.question: [B2+ • Negative Inversion] «Ледве ми сіли за стіл, як згасло світло» — Hardly ___ sat down at the table when the lights went out.
questions.explanation: Інверсія після 'Hardly ... when': допоміжне дієслово Past Perfect ('had') ставиться ПЕРЕД підметом ('had we sat down').
questions.hintText: Інверсія: Hardly + had + Subject + V3 ... when.

questions.question: [B2+ • Negative Inversion] «Щойно він підписав контракт, як зрозумів свою помилку» — No sooner had he signed the contract ___ he realised his mistake.
questions.explanation: У конструкції 'No sooner ... than' завжди вживається сполучник порівняння 'than' (через 'a'!), тоді як з 'Hardly/Scarcely' вживається 'when'.
questions.hintText: Стійка пара: No sooner ... ___ (порівняльний сполучник через 'a').

questions.question: [B2+ • Impersonal Reporting Passive] «Повідомляють, що компанія втратила мільйони минулого кварталу» — The company is reported ___ millions last quarter.
questions.explanation: Оскільки втрата коштів відбулася в минулому ('last quarter') раніше за саме повідомлення, після пасиву 'is reported' вживається перфектний інфінітив: 'to have + V3' (to have lost).
questions.hintText: Дія в минулому після is reported/believed: to have + V3.

questions.question: [B2+ • Mixed Conditional (Reverse)] «Якби вона не боялася висоти (взагалі), вона б піднялася з нами на вежу вчора» — If she weren't afraid of heights, she ___ the tower with us yesterday.
questions.explanation: Зворотний Mixed Conditional (постійний стан зараз → наслідок у минулому 'yesterday'): If + Past Simple (weren't), would have + V3 (would have climbed).
questions.hintText: Наслідок учора ('yesterday') вимагає would have + V3!

questions.question: [B2+ • Subjunctive Mood] «Юрист наполягав, щоб кожен свідок був присутній на слуханні» — The lawyer insisted that every witness ___ present at the hearing.
questions.explanation: Present Subjunctive: після 'insist / demand / recommend / essential that' вживається початкова форма дієслова (bare infinitive) для всіх осіб — 'be' (або 'should be').
questions.hintText: Subjunctive після insist that: початкова форма дієслова (be).

questions.question: [B2+ • Past Modals of Deduction] «Дорога мокра — вночі, напевно, йшов дощ» — The road is wet; it ___ during the night.
questions.optionsString: must have rained|should have rained|can't have rained|needn't have rained
questions.explanation: Логічний висновок із майже 100% впевненістю щодо минулої дії на основі наявних доказів ('The road is wet') передається через 'must have + V3'.
questions.hintText: Впевнене логічне припущення про минуле: must have + V3.

questions.question: [B2+ • Inversion with Not Only] «Він не лише запізнився, а й забув документи» — Not only ___ late, but he also forgot the documents.
questions.optionsString: was he|he was|did he be|has he
questions.explanation: Коли речення починається з 'Not only', у першій частині відбувається інверсія (як у питанні): 'Not only was he late...'.
questions.hintText: Після початкового 'Not only' дієслово 'was' ставиться перед підметом 'he'.

questions.question: [B2+ • Regret + V-ing vs to V] «Ми з прикрістю повідомляємо вам, що ваш рейс затримано» — We regret ___ you that your flight has been delayed.
questions.explanation: В офіційних повідомленнях ('з прикрістю повідомляємо зараз') вживається 'regret + to V' (to inform / to say / to announce). 'regret + V-ing' означає жаль про минулу дію.
questions.hintText: Офіційне повідомлення поганої новини зараз: regret + to V.

questions.question: [B2+ • Phrasal Verbs] «Команді вдалося придумати геніальне рішення в останню хвилину» — The team managed to ___ a brilliant solution at the last minute.
questions.optionsString: come up with|put up with|do away with|get away with
questions.explanation: 'come up with' = придумати, знайти ідею чи рішення; 'get away with' = уникнути покарання; 'do away with' = позбутися, скасувати.
questions.hintText: Придумати ідею/рішення = come ___ ___.

questions.question: [B2+ • Wish / If Only Past Regret] «Як шкода, що я не послухав твоєї поради минулого тижня!» — If only I ___ to your advice last week!
questions.explanation: Жаль про минулу дію ('last week') після 'If only' або 'I wish' вимагає Past Perfect: had + V3 (had listened).
questions.hintText: Жаль щодо минулого після If only / I wish: had + V3.
